commands.name: go-linter-driven-development:documentation
commands.description:
(go-linter-driven-development) The repo-brain author/maintainer: writes behavior-focused documentation and wires it
into the documentation network defined by rules/R9-repo-brain.md.
FEATURE mode (default): after feature implementation or bug fixes — invoked by
@linter-driven-development (Phase 5) — to document HOW THE PRODUCT BEHAVES and wire
it into the network.
BOOTSTRAP mode: on request ("set up docs", "create an index", "make this repo
AI-navigable", /wire-repo-brain) or when FEATURE mode finds no doc root — discovers
the doc root, verifies-or-adds OKF frontmatter, builds index.md, wires
CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, wires missing code→docs edges, installs conventions.md and
the conformance check script, reports gaps.
NOT a changelog - documents current behavior, not change history.

commands.name: go-linter-driven-development:linter-driven-development
commands.description:
(go-linter-driven-development) META ORCHESTRATOR for any Go code change that should end in a commit (features, bug fixes, refactors).
WHEN: User requests Go code work (implement, fix, add, refactor), mentions "@ldd"/"ldd", or runs a /go-ldd-* command in a Go project.
Runs the five-phase workflow (PREPARE is an autonomous sub-phase, 1.5): DESIGN → PREPARE → IMPLEMENT (per-behavior TDD loop) → FULL LINT (lint-fixer agent) → REVIEW (per slice) → SHIP.

commands.name: go-linter-driven-development:pre-commit-review
commands.description:
(go-linter-driven-development) ADVISORY pre-commit review that orchestrates parallel single-obsession rule hunters, an over-abstraction skeptic, and a comment critic against the diff.
Spawns read-only agents (rule-hunter, overabstraction-skeptic, comment-critic); NEVER edits code.
Invoked by @linter-driven-development (Phase 4), by @refactoring (after pattern application), or manually for standalone code review.
Categorizes findings as Bugs, New Practice (when in Rome), Design Debt, Readability Debt, or Polish Opportunities. Does NOT block commits.

commands.name: go-linter-driven-development:refactoring
commands.description:
(go-linter-driven-development) BACKWARD view over rules/ — routes linter and review failures to the rule whose Fix pattern owns the repair.
Use when linter fails with complexity issues (cyclomatic, cognitive, maintainability) or when code feels hard to read/maintain.
Also runs PREPARATORY mode: reshape code an approved plan touches, before the first RED, so the feature lands add-only.
Applies storifying, type extraction, function extraction, conditional-dispatch, and mutation-discipline patterns via rules/R1-R8 and R10-R12.

commands.name: go-linter-driven-development:testing
commands.description:
(go-linter-driven-development) Use when creating leaf types, after refactoring, during implementation, or when testing advice is needed.
Automatically invoked to write tests for new types, or use as testing expert advisor.
Covers the composition ladder from rung-0 unit tests to whole-system tests, with emphasis on real in-memory dependencies.
Ensures 100% coverage on leaf types with public API testing.

commands.name: design
commands.description: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: artifact-diagramming
commands.description: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

commands.name: artifact-capabilities
commands.description: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify

commands.name: build-sales-content
commands.description: Generate on-brand, field-ready WEKA sales content from a Marketing-approved content sandbox. Use this skill whenever a seller needs to create a one-pager, email, sales deck, executive brief, discovery prep sheet, or LinkedIn post — or wants to convert/rebrand existing sales collateral into the current WEKA template. Trigger when the user says "build", "create", "write", "draft", "generate", "convert", "rebrand", or describes any sales content need. Also triggers when the user pastes existing copy for a brand/product compliance review. Covers guided intake (audience, use case, competitor), proof point selection from the validated registry, and rendered output via weka-doc-builder (.docx) or weka-deck-builder (.pptx). (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: convert-to-weka-doc
commands.description: Convert existing WEKA content (Word, Google Doc, markdown, or PDF) into the current WEKA-branded Word template. Use whenever someone has older WEKA collateral — Solution Brief, White Paper, Reference Architecture, Data Sheet, Service Guide, or any other type — and wants it refreshed into the current template. Trigger on phrases like "convert this PDF", "rebrand this old doc", "migrate this Solution Brief into the new template", "update this doc to current branding", "convert this to a Word doc in our template", or any time a user uploads legacy WEKA content alongside a request to bring it forward. The skill extracts source structure, walks the user through a recast conversation to map content into the doc-builder spec, then hands off to weka-doc-builder to render the final .docx. It does NOT fix voice, tone, or claims — for that, recommend `is-this-on-brand` after conversion. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: convert-to-weka-slides
commands.description: Convert existing decks (PowerPoint, Google Slides export, Keynote export, or PDF slide export) into the current WEKA-branded PowerPoint template. Use whenever someone has a legacy deck — old pitch deck, sales presentation, customer deck, executive briefing, conference talk slides — and wants it refreshed into the current template and layouts. Trigger on phrases like "convert this deck", "rebrand this old presentation", "migrate this pptx to our new template", "update these slides to current branding", "redo this in the WEKA template", "modernize this deck", or any time a user uploads a legacy deck alongside a request to bring it forward. The skill extracts source slides, walks the user through a recast conversation to map each slide to the closest current layout, then hands off to weka-deck-builder to render the final .pptx. It does NOT fix copy quality, voice, or claim accuracy — for that, recommend `is-this-on-brand` after conversion. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers a dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

(claude.ai sync)

commands.name: is-this-on-brand
commands.description: Audit any WEKA content piece against the Brand Voice & Writing Style Guide. Use this skill whenever a user pastes copy, a draft, a headline, a LinkedIn post, an email, a product page, slide copy, or any piece of writing and asks if it's on-brand, needs review, sounds right, follows WEKA style, or should be approved. Also trigger when the user says "check this," "does this sound like us," "is this ready to publish," "review my copy," or pastes content without a question — they almost certainly want a brand review. Trigger for any content described as a WEKA blog, email, social post, deck slide, webpage, UX string, press release, data sheet, or case study. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: morning

commands.description: Render WEKA-branded PowerPoint decks (.pptx) by applying content to the locked WEKA Corporate Default template. Triggers when another skill (build-sales-content, marketing-content, hope-update-writer) has finished producing copy and needs to put it on slides; also use directly when someone has rough copy to lay out. Trigger phrases include "build the deck", "make this a deck", "render as slides", "drop this into the WEKA template", "put together a sales deck", "make a pitch deck". Also exports the full template as a labeled 40-slide layout gallery for users who want "a clean template", "the WEKA template", "all the layouts in one file", or a reference deck — use the `--export-template` flag. This skill handles the layout and brand layer only — content quality, voice, and approval are the calling skill's job. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: weka-doc-builder
commands.description: Render WEKA-branded short-form and long-form Word documents (.docx) by applying content to the locked WEKA templates. Use this skill whenever the final output is a WEKA Solution Brief, Data Sheet, Executive Brief, Technical Brief, Technical Spotlight, One Pager, White Paper, Customer Case Study, Reference Architecture, Solution Architecture, Process Guide, Product Documentation, or Service Guide. Also use when another skill (build-sales-content, marketing-content, hope-update-writer, or anything writing on-brand WEKA collateral) has finished generating content and needs to put it on the page. Trigger on phrases like "build the doc", "render this as a Solution Brief", "make this a WEKA white paper", "drop this into the template", or any time WEKA-branded copy needs to land in the official Word template. This skill handles the layout and brand layer only — content quality, voice, and approval are the calling skill's job. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: weka-group-manager
commands.description: Answer any question about WEKA's Google distribution lists (DLs) and groups using the WEKA Group Manager MCP connector. Use this skill whenever a user asks about: finding the right DL/group to email or schedule a meeting with, discovering which DLs/groups a person belongs to, understanding how a group's membership rules work, or looking up employee attributes like department, team, manager, site, or job level. "DL", "distribution list", "group", and "mailing list" are all synonyms — treat them identically. Trigger this skill for any phrasing like "what group should I use for...", "which DL covers...", "who is in...", "what groups is [name] in", "how is [group] defined", "what are the rules for...", "tell me about [employee]", "who reports to...", "find me a list for...", or any question about sending emails or scheduling meetings with a set of WEKA employees. Always prefer this skill over guessing or answering from memory. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Base directory for this skill: /home/user/ai-coding-rules/go-linter-driven-development/skills/pre-commit-review

<objective>
Verify a finished diff against the plugin's rules (R1–R12) with evidence, by orchestrating
parallel single-obsession `rule-hunter` agents, one `overabstraction-skeptic`, and one
`comment-critic`.
Pure orchestration and reporting: this skill may spawn agents but never edits code, never
fixes findings, and never blocks a commit. Rule knowledge lives once in `../../rules/`;
agents receive it as spawn-time payload — they do not invoke skills.
</objective>

<timing>
Run pre-commit, per completed vertical slice — NEVER mid-implementation. GREEN-step TDD
code is supposed to look under-designed; reviewing it produces false positives. The
per-cycle detection greps in the REFACTOR step (see @refactoring) are the
mid-implementation net; this pass is the verification net on finished work.
</timing>

<inputs>
- **Diff scope**: staged changes by default (`git diff --cached --name-only -- '*.go'`),
  or an explicit file list / diff range from the caller.
- **Mode**: `FULL` (first run) or `INCREMENTAL` (re-run after fixes — requires the
  previous report's findings).
</inputs>

<protocol>

<step_1_grep_prefilter>
In-context, cheap — no agents yet. For each rule below, read its rule file's
**Falsifying questions** section and run the detection commands there against the diff
scope (changed files only). The commands live in the rule files; never restate them here.
A rule with zero hits is skipped — no hunter spawned for it.

| Rule | File | Hunt focus |
|------|------|------------|
| R1 | `../../rules/R1-primitive-obsession.md` | domain concepts as raw primitives; sentinel returns; ceremony wrappers (inverse) |
| R2 | `../../rules/R2-self-validating-types.md` | invalid-state construction; defensive re-checks; nil as a value |
| R3 | `../../rules/R3-storifying.md` | mixed abstraction levels; comments naming unextracted blocks |
| R4 | `../../rules/R4-helper-placement.md` | helper visibility/placement off the placement ladder |
| R5 | `../../rules/R5-vertical-slice.md` | horizontal layering; role-named packages |
| R6 | `../../rules/R6-test-only-interfaces.md` | interfaces whose only second implementer is a test double |
| R7 | `../../rules/R7-test-placement.md` | internal test packages; wantErr conditionals; wrong-rung tests; sleeps |
| R8 | `../../rules/R8-no-globals.md` | package-level state; `context.Background()` in library code |
| R9 | `../../rules/R9-repo-brain.md` | orphan docs; broken doc edges (both directions); WHAT-comments on exported API; unwired root; bundle-contract breaks (missing frontmatter, index timestamps, log.md) |
| R10 | `../../rules/R10-concurrency-safety.md` | goroutines without exit paths or owners; unguarded shared-state writes; production sleeps; decorative mutexes |
| R11 | `../../rules/R11-conditional-dispatch.md` | one discriminator switched in ≥2 places; type switches in domain logic; unknown-kind defaults away from the boundary; flag arguments; unearned dispatch abstractions (inverse) |
| R12 | `../../rules/R12-mutation-discipline.md` | internal slices/maps returned by reference; constructors aliasing caller collections; query/modifier hybrids; setters around validating constructors; ceremony copies (inverse) |

Also in-context: a new `//nolint` directive or `.golangci.yaml` exclusion in the diff is
itself a finding — the change must justify, with evidence, that the rule genuinely does
not apply.

Also in-context — the **when-in-Rome check**: a diff must arrive in the host repo's
existing style, not import a new one. Flag anything the diff introduces that the repo
does not already use: a new test mechanism (golden files, snapshot testing, a new
assertion library), a new dependency in `go.mod`, a new tool or config file, edits to
repo-level convention files (CLAUDE.md, coding standards, lint config) bundled into a
feature diff, or a directory layout unlike its siblings. Detection is comparative:
for each candidate, grep the repo *outside* the diff for prior use — zero prior use
is the finding. These are not style crimes; they are adoption decisions that belong
to the repo owner. The fix is a discussion or a separate PR, never silent inclusion.
</step_1_grep_prefilter>

<step_2_spawn_hunters>
For every rule with pre-filter hits, spawn one `rule-hunter` agent — all hunters in a
single message, in parallel. Each spawn prompt MUST contain:

1. **The rule file's FULL content, pasted** — the hunter's entire rulebook and single
   obsession. Never a path reference alone; never more than one rule per hunter.
2. **The diff scope** — the changed-file list or `git diff` range.
3. **That rule's pre-filter hits** — as starting leads (the hunter re-runs the
   detection commands itself; leads are a starting point, not a limit).

If the rule cites a case file by plugin-relative path (e.g. `../examples/*.md`), resolve
it to an absolute path and include that path in the spawn prompt — the hunter runs in the
reviewed project's cwd and cannot resolve plugin-relative paths on its own.

Each hunter returns one block per finding:
`rule | file:line | evidence (falsifying-question answers) | proposed fix pattern | effort (S/M/L)`
plus a final tally line (`R<N>: <M> finding(s)` or a hunted-clean line).
</step_2_spawn_hunters>

<step_3_skeptic_pass>
Collect ALL type/package-extraction findings — every R1/R2/R4 "create a type/package"
proposal, R10 "Extract Synchronized Owner" proposals, and R11 "Interface Dispatch" /
"Strategy Map" proposals — and spawn one `overabstraction-skeptic`. Its spawn prompt MUST contain:

1. The extraction findings under review — the hunter blocks pasted verbatim.
2. Payload: the **Juiciness scoring** and **The over-abstraction trap** sections of
   `../../rules/R1-primitive-obsession.md`, pasted.
3. Payload: the FULL content of `../../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md`, pasted.

Verdicts per finding: `CONFIRMED (score + verified evidence)` or
`REFUTED (score 0–1 + reason) → cheaper alternative`. A refuted proposal does not ship;
when its cheaper alternative (better naming, private fields + accessors, or R11's
Keep the Single Exhaustive Switch) is still worth doing, report the alternative as
🟢 Polish. When R11 dispatch proposals are under review, additionally paste the FULL
content of both R11 case files — `../../examples/anti-if-dispatch.md` (Move 3 is the
juiciness rejection: the switch stays, goes exhaustive) and
`../../examples/switch-to-polymorphism.md` (the dependency-direction rejection: the
move is unavailable when the consumer owns the output format; the switch shrinks to
pure dispatch). Only findings the skeptic cannot kill ship as extraction
findings. Non-extraction findings (R3, R5–R9, and R1/R2/R10/R11 findings that propose
no new type) skip the skeptic and go straight to the report — R9 findings (orphans,
broken edges, WHAT-comments, unwired root) propose no type extractions.
</step_3_skeptic_pass>

<step_3b_comment_critic>
When the diff contains comment lines — prefilter:
`git diff --cached -- '*.go' | grep -E '^\+.*//' | grep -vE '//(go:|nolint| Output:)'`
(any hit qualifies; directives don't count) — spawn one `comment-critic` alongside
the skeptic (same message when both run). Its spawn prompt MUST contain:

1. Payload: R9's **Comment policy** section (`../../rules/R9-repo-brain.md`,
   Design guidance) pasted verbatim — the Comment Value Toolbox kinds, the
   three-test standard, the tier table, budget accounting, and the visibility
   default.
2. Payload: the **Comment Value Toolbox** catalog section of
   `../documentation/reference.md` (resolve to an absolute path) pasted verbatim.
3. The absolute path to `../../examples/private-comment-noise.md` — the critic
   reads it when judging comments on unexported symbols.
4. The diff scope.

It judges every comment in the diff (godoc, in-body, test) against the three-test
standard and returns per-comment verdicts (`KEEP / TRIM / REWRITE / DELETE`, or
`DELETE → route R3` for in-body extraction candidates) with evidence and proposed
replacement text. Non-KEEP verdicts land in the report as 🟡 Readability Debt;
`DELETE → route R3` verdicts merge with any R3 hunter findings on the same lines
(one finding, not two). The critic is advisory like everything else — accepted
verdicts are fixed by @documentation (the rung-1 fixer), except R3 routes, which
go to @refactoring.
</step_3b_comment_critic>

<step_4_merged_report>
Merge surviving findings into one report.

**Cluster pass (before categorizing):** group surviving findings by shared anchor —
the same type, field/discriminator, or function named in ≥2 findings from *different*
rules. Each hunter is single-obsession and blind to the others, so independent
convergence on one anchor is evidence that a domain concept is missing there — the
cluster is a juiciness scorecard that filled itself in (R1 hunter sees the raw
primitive, R11 the duplicated switch, R2 the ownerless validation: one disease, four
jurisdictions). Render each cluster as a first-class entry above the categories:

```
🔗 CLUSTER: Alert.Channel (4 findings: R1, R11, R2, R7)
   Hypothesis: missing domain concept — a Channel type wants to exist
   Routing: design-first — @code-designing (cluster-scoped), then @refactoring
   implements; do NOT fix members independently (partial fixes undo each other)
```

Member findings still appear under their categories below, tagged
`[cluster: <anchor>]`. Clustering is *reporting* — this skill still never edits and
never invokes fix skills; the caller routes.

Category mapping:

- 🐛 **Bugs** — will fail at runtime regardless of rule (nil returned as a value,
  cancellation swallowed by `context.Background()`, R10 goroutine leaks and
  unguarded concurrent writes): fix immediately.
- 🟠 **New Practice (when in Rome)** — the when-in-Rome check's findings: a
  mechanism, dependency, framework, or convention the host repo does not already
  use, introduced without discussion. Advisory like everything else, but flag it
  loudly: reviewers reject these threads hardest, and the fix (owner buy-in or a
  separate PR) is cheap before pushing and expensive after.
- 🔴 **Design Debt** — R1, R2, R4, R6, R7, R8, R10's non-crash findings (production
  sleeps, fire-and-forget ownership, mutex placement), R11 (duplicated discriminators,
  boundary leaks), R12 (leaked mutable internals, unvalidated setters), and R5
  (advisory — never blocks; the user may have valid reasons): fix before commit
  recommended.
- 🟡 **Readability Debt** — R3, R9, unclear naming, and the comment-critic's
  non-KEEP verdicts (trash or over-budget or hard-to-read comments): improves
  maintainability.
- 🟢 **Polish** — minor idiomatic improvements, the skeptic's cheaper alternatives.

Every finding carries evidence — `file:line` plus the falsifying-question answer or
command output — never a bare verdict. Effort carries over from the hunter (S/M/L).
Fix routing is each rule file's **Fix pattern** section; cite it, don't restate it.
Issues noticed outside the diff scope go in a BROADER CONTEXT section, not as findings.
</step_4_merged_report>

</protocol>

content.content:
1	# R1 — Primitive Obsession
2	
3	## Principle
4	
5	Domain concepts must not travel as raw `string`/`int`/`bool`/`[]T`. When a primitive
6	carries validation rules, behavior, or a domain name, it becomes a type with a
7	validating constructor and named methods. The inverse binds equally: a wrapper that
8	adds no validation, no logic, and no invariant is over-abstraction — score before you wrap.
9	
10	## Why
11	
12	A rule enforced on a primitive is enforced at every call site and owned by none: the
13	check gets duplicated, drifts, and is skipped exactly once — in the code path that
14	ships the bug. Logic trapped on primitives is also untestable in isolation: you must
15	construct whatever large object happens to hold the primitive. A domain type gives the
16	rule one owner (the constructor — see `R2-self-validating-types.md`), gives the
17	behavior a name, makes invalid values unrepresentable downstream, and turns the logic
18	into a leaf that unit-tests with literals. Where the extracted type then lives is
19	`R4-helper-placement.md`.
20	
21	## Canonical example
22	
23	Real PR code (weka/goweka#951). `kubeService` wraps a Kubernetes Service DTO and must
24	pick the management port: prefer the port named `weka-api`, else fall back to the
25	first valid port.
26	
27	### Before
28	
29	```go
30	func (s kubeService) managementPort() int32 {
31	    for _, p := range s.Spec.Ports {
32	        if p.Name == "weka-api" && p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535 {
33	            return p.Port
34	        }
35	    }
36	    for _, p := range s.Spec.Ports {
37	        if p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535 {
38	            return p.Port
39	        }
40	    }
41	    return 0
42	}
43	```
44	
45	Four defects in twelve lines:
46	
47	- The validity rule `p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535` is duplicated across the two
48	  loops — two copies that can drift independently.
49	- Two abstractions exist only as unnamed boolean expressions: "valid port" and
50	  "named management port".
51	- The logic lives on a K8s DTO, so it is testable only by constructing a
52	  `kubeService` around a full Service object.
53	- `return 0` is a sentinel: validity is encoded in-band, and every caller must know
54	  that `0` means "none".
55	
56	### Stage 1 — self-validating types with constructors
57	
58	```go
59	// ServicePort is the wire DTO. Its fields stay exported with json tags —
60	// unexported fields with json tags silently fail to unmarshal (encoding/json
61	// skips them without error, and every port reads as zero).
62	type ServicePort struct {
63	    Name string `json:"name"`
64	    Port int32  `json:"port"`
65	}
66	
67	// Port is a named, validated service port. It cannot exist out of range,
68	// so no downstream code ever re-checks it.
69	type Port struct {
70	    name   string
71	    number int32
72	}
73	
74	func ParsePort(name string, number int32) (Port, error) {
75	    if number <= 0 || number > 65535 {
76	        return Port{}, fmt.Errorf("port %q: %d out of range 1-65535", name, number)
77	    }
78	    return Port{name: name, number: number}, nil
79	}
80	
81	func (p Port) Name() string  { return p.name }
82	func (p Port) Number() int32 { return p.number }
83	
84	// Ports is a collection of valid ports.
85	type Ports []Port
86	
87	// ParsePorts drops invalid wire entries — a documented decision that mirrors
88	// the original skip-and-fall-back semantics: an invalid port was never chosen
89	// before; now it never exists.
90	func ParsePorts(wire []ServicePort) Ports {
91	    ports := make(Ports, 0, len(wire))
92	    for _, w := range wire {
93	        p, err := ParsePort(w.Name, w.Port)
94	        if err != nil {
95	            continue
96	        }
97	        ports = append(ports, p)
98	    }
99	    return ports
100	}
101	
102	func (ps Ports) FirstNamed(name string) (Port, bool) {
103	    for _, p := range ps {
104	        if p.name == name {
105	            return p, true
106	        }
107	    }
108	    return Port{}, false
109	}
110	
111	func (ps Ports) First() (Port, bool) {
112	    if len(ps) == 0 {
113	        return Port{}, false
114	    }
115	    return ps[0], true
116	}
117	
118	// Management prefers the port named "weka-api", else the first valid port.
119	// (Stage 2 relocates this method — the "weka-api" preference is feature
120	// policy, not networking vocabulary.)
121	func (ps Ports) Management() (Port, bool) {
122	    if p, ok := ps.FirstNamed("weka-api"); ok {
123	        return p, true
124	    }
125	    return ps.First()
126	}

# R1 — Primitive Obsession

## Principle

Domain concepts must not travel as raw `string`/`int`/`bool`/`[]T`. When a primitive
carries validation rules, behavior, or a domain name, it becomes a type with a
validating constructor and named methods. The inverse binds equally: a wrapper that
adds no validation, no logic, and no invariant is over-abstraction — score before you wrap.

## Why

A rule enforced on a primitive is enforced at every call site and owned by none: the
check gets duplicated, drifts, and is skipped exactly once — in the code path that
ships the bug. Logic trapped on primitives is also untestable in isolation: you must
construct whatever large object happens to hold the primitive. A domain type gives the
rule one owner (the constructor — see `R2-self-validating-types.md`), gives the
behavior a name, makes invalid values unrepresentable downstream, and turns the logic
into a leaf that unit-tests with literals. Where the extracted type then lives is
`R4-helper-placement.md`.

## Canonical example

Real PR code (weka/goweka#951). `kubeService` wraps a Kubernetes Service DTO and must
pick the management port: prefer the port named `weka-api`, else fall back to the
first valid port.

### Before

```go
func (s kubeService) managementPort() int32 {
    for _, p := range s.Spec.Ports {
        if p.Name == "weka-api" && p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535 {
            return p.Port
        }
    }
    for _, p := range s.Spec.Ports {
        if p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535 {
            return p.Port
        }
    }
    return 0
}
```

Four defects in twelve lines:

- The validity rule `p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535` is duplicated across the two
  loops — two copies that can drift independently.
- Two abstractions exist only as unnamed boolean expressions: "valid port" and
  "named management port".
- The logic lives on a K8s DTO, so it is testable only by constructing a
  `kubeService` around a full Service object.
- `return 0` is a sentinel: validity is encoded in-band, and every caller must know
  that `0` means "none".

### Stage 1 — self-validating types with constructors

```go
// ServicePort is the wire DTO. Its fields stay exported with json tags —
// unexported fields with json tags silently fail to unmarshal (encoding/json
// skips them without error, and every port reads as zero).
type ServicePort struct {
    Name string `json:"name"`
    Port int32  `json:"port"`
}

// Port is a named, validated service port. It cannot exist out of range,
// so no downstream code ever re-checks it.
type Port struct {
    name   string
    number int32
}

func ParsePort(name string, number int32) (Port, error) {
    if number <= 0 || number > 65535 {
        return Port{}, fmt.Errorf("port %q: %d out of range 1-65535", name, number)
    }
    return Port{name: name, number: number}, nil
}

func (p Port) Name() string  { return p.name }
func (p Port) Number() int32 { return p.number }

// Ports is a collection of valid ports.
type Ports []Port

// ParsePorts drops invalid wire entries — a documented decision that mirrors
// the original skip-and-fall-back semantics: an invalid port was never chosen
// before; now it never exists.
func ParsePorts(wire []ServicePort) Ports {
    ports := make(Ports, 0, len(wire))
    for _, w := range wire {
        p, err := ParsePort(w.Name, w.Port)
        if err != nil {
            continue
        }
        ports = append(ports, p)
    }
    return ports
}

func (ps Ports) FirstNamed(name string) (Port, bool) {
    for _, p := range ps {
        if p.name == name {
            return p, true
        }
    }
    return Port{}, false
}

func (ps Ports) First() (Port, bool) {
    if len(ps) == 0 {
        return Port{}, false
    }
    return ps[0], true
}

// Management prefers the port named "weka-api", else the first valid port.
// (Stage 2 relocates this method — the "weka-api" preference is feature
// policy, not networking vocabulary.)
func (ps Ports) Management() (Port, bool) {
    if p, ok := ps.FirstNamed("weka-api"); ok {
        return p, true
    }
    return ps.First()
}
```

The payoff, stated plainly: notice what was **not** written. There is no `IsValid()`
method and no validity loop anywhere. Self-validation does not move the
`> 0 && <= 65535` check somewhere tidier — it **deletes the concept of a
maybe-invalid port from downstream logic**. Every `Port` inside a `Ports` is valid by
construction, so "find the first valid port" collapses to "find the first port". And
`Management()` returns `(Port, bool)` comma-ok — never a `0` sentinel that smuggles
validity back in-band.

### Stage 2 — placement (R4 rung 3)

`Port`, `Ports`, `FirstNamed`, `First` say nothing about Kubernetes or Weka — they
are generic networking vocabulary, so they move to `internal/pkg/networking`
(rung 3 of `R4-helper-placement.md`). The wire adapter `ParsePorts` knows the K8s
DTO, so it stays with the feature. The feature policy stays home as a four-line
storified method:

```go
func (s kubeService) managementPort() (networking.Port, bool) {
    if p, ok := s.ports.FirstNamed(kubeWekaAPIPort); ok { return p, true }
    return s.ports.First()
}
```

Teaching point: **promote only the domain-generic parts.** The `"weka-api"` constant
is feature policy and stays in the feature — a shared package that knows one
feature's port names is not shared vocabulary, it is leaked policy.

### Stage 3 — testing contrast

Before, exercising `managementPort()` meant constructing a `kubeService` around a
full Service fixture — building a Kubernetes object to check a range predicate.
After, the logic is a leaf and its rung-0 unit tests (the composition ladder's
bottom rung — see @testing) are slice literals against `networking.Ports`; no
big-object construction:

```go
func TestPorts_FirstNamed(t *testing.T) {
    api := mustPort(t, "weka-api", 14000)
    web := mustPort(t, "http", 80)

    got, ok := networking.Ports{web, api}.FirstNamed("weka-api")

    require.True(t, ok)
    assert.Equal(t, api, got)
}

func mustPort(t *testing.T, name string, number int32) networking.Port {
    t.Helper()
    p, err := networking.ParsePort(name, number)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    return p
}
```

### The opposite failure: don't over-extract

```go
// ❌ Ceremony, not a type: no rule, no behavior — the only method unwraps.
type ReplicaCount int

func (c ReplicaCount) Int() int { return int(c) }
```

Score it against the scorecard below: no validation (+0), no meaningful methods (+0),
one call site (+0) → Score 0. Keep the `int`; if you want a name, a well-named
variable or an unexported helper in the same package is the whole answer
(`R4-helper-placement.md`, rung 1). Deep worked rejection with the cheaper
alternatives: `../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md`.

## Design guidance

A primitive should become a type when it has validation rules, has behavior attached,
represents a domain concept, is used in multiple places, or when passing an invalid
value would be a bug. When the call is not obvious, score it.

### Juiciness scoring

This scorecard lives here and only here — other rules and skills cite it, never
restate it.

**Behavioral (rich behavior):**
- Complex validation (regex, ranges, business rules): +3
- Multiple meaningful methods (≥2): +2
- State transitions/transformations: +2
- Format conversions: +1

**Structural (organizing complexity):**
- Parsing unstructured data into fields: +3
- Grouping related data that travels together: +2
- Making implicit structure explicit: +2
- Replacing `map[string]interface{}`: +2

**Usage (simplifies code):**
- Used in 5+ places: +2
- Used in 3-4 places: +1
- Significantly simplifies calling code: +1
- Makes tests cleaner: +1

**Verdict:**
- Score ≥4: HIGH priority — clear win, create the type.
- Score 2-3: MEDIUM priority — judgment call, present to the user.
- Score 0-1: LOW priority — do not create the type; that is over-engineering.

### The over-abstraction trap

The failure mode symmetric to primitive obsession is wrapping a primitive that has
nothing to own: no validation, no invariant, one method that merely unwraps. The
honest test: is `x.Field.IsSet()` *significantly* clearer than a well-named field or
accessor? If the real need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic,
private fields with accessors beat a wrapper type. Deep worked case — the tried
extraction, the rejection rationale, and the cheaper alternatives:
`../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md`.

### Placement

A juicy type must also land in the right package — feature-scoped versus
domain-generic. That decision is `R4-helper-placement.md`; the canonical example's
Stage 2 shows it applied.

## Fix pattern

- **Replace Primitive with Domain Type**: introduce `ParseX(raw) (X, error)`
  (`R2-self-validating-types.md`); migrate call sites so raw values cross into `X`
  exactly once, at the boundary.
- **Extract Collection Type**: when logic loops over `[]primitive` or `[]DTO`, wrap
  the slice (`type Ports []Port`) and move the loop into a named query method.
- **Replace Sentinel with comma-ok**: `return 0` / `return ""` meaning
  absence/invalidity → `(X, bool)` or `(X, error)`.
- **Name enum strings**: `if status == "READY"` → `type Status string` with
  `const StatusReady Status = "READY"`.
- **Introduce Parameter Object** (Fowler): the same group of parameters traveling
  through multiple signatures (`host string, port int, useTLS bool`) becomes one
  type — that is the scorecard's "grouping related data that travels together" made
  concrete. Prefer passing the whole object over re-exploding its fields at the next
  call (Preserve Whole Object).
- **Over-abstraction found instead?** Apply the cheaper alternative — better naming,
  or private fields + accessors — per `../examples/overabstraction-cidr.md`.
- Multi-rule refactoring procedure (sequencing extraction with storifying):
  `../skills/refactoring/reference.md`. Forward design of the new types:
  @code-designing.

## Falsifying questions

Answer each with evidence (`file:line`, command output) — never a bare verdict.

1. **Does the diff validate a primitive inline instead of constructing a type?**
   Detection: `grep -nE 'if [a-zA-Z_.]+ (==|!=) ""|if [a-zA-Z_.]+ (<=?|>=?) [0-9]' $(git diff --name-only -- '*.go')`
   Violation: an emptiness/range/format check on a parameter or DTO field that names

2. **Is the same predicate enforced in more than one place?**

   Violation: ≥2 hits — the rule has no single owner; a type is missing.

3. **Does named behavior run on a bare primitive?** Loops/switches over `[]string`,

   Violation: behavior attached to a bare primitive where a named method on a type
   would carry it.

4. **Does any function return a sentinel to mean "not found / invalid"?**

   whose signature has no `bool` or `error` result.
   Violation: validity encoded in-band — requires comma-ok or `(X, error)`.

5. **Do the same parameters travel together across signatures?**

1	# R2 — Self-Validating Types
2	
3	## Principle
4	
5	A type validates its own invariants in its constructor — the only way to obtain a
6	value — and every method thereafter trusts the receiver. Validation ownership never
7	sits upstream: a type that relies on callers to have validated for it is not
8	self-validating, whatever its fields look like.
9	
10	## Why
11	
12	Constructor validation makes invalid values unrepresentable. Without it, every method
13	must defend against bad state, forgetting one check is a latent panic, and the
14	defensive noise buries the actual logic. With it, nil-checks, emptiness checks, and
15	range checks vanish from the entire downstream call graph — the payoff compounds with
16	every method and every caller. Errors also surface at the boundary where the bad data
17	entered, carrying context, instead of deep in an unrelated call stack.
18	
19	## Canonical example
20	
21	Compact excerpt from the Port case (`R1-primitive-obsession.md` has the full
22	three-stage study — extraction, placement, testing):
23	
24	```go
25	// Port cannot exist out of range — the constructor is the only entry.
26	type Port struct {
27	    name   string
28	    number int32
29	}
30	
31	func ParsePort(name string, number int32) (Port, error) {
32	    if number <= 0 || number > 65535 {
33	        return Port{}, fmt.Errorf("port %q: %d out of range 1-65535", name, number)
34	    }
35	    return Port{name: name, number: number}, nil
36	}
37	```
38	
39	Before this type existed, `p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535` was duplicated across two
40	loops at the use site. After, there is no `IsValid()` and no re-check anywhere: the
41	concept of a maybe-invalid port is deleted from downstream logic, not relocated.
42	
43	The same pattern for a composed object — validate dependencies once, then trust:
44	
45	```go
46	// ❌ every method defends
47	type UserService struct {
48	    Repo Repository // exported, might be nil
49	}
50	
51	func (s *UserService) CreateUser(ctx context.Context, u User) error {
52	    if s.Repo == nil { // repeated in every method; forget one → panic
53	        return errors.New("repo is nil")
54	    }
55	    return s.Repo.Save(ctx, u)
56	}
57

# R2 — Self-Validating Types

## Principle

A type validates its own invariants in its constructor — the only way to obtain a
value — and every method thereafter trusts the receiver. Validation ownership never
sits upstream: a type that relies on callers to have validated for it is not
self-validating, whatever its fields look like.

## Why

Constructor validation makes invalid values unrepresentable. Without it, every method
must defend against bad state, forgetting one check is a latent panic, and the
defensive noise buries the actual logic. With it, nil-checks, emptiness checks, and
range checks vanish from the entire downstream call graph — the payoff compounds with
every method and every caller. Errors also surface at the boundary where the bad data
entered, carrying context, instead of deep in an unrelated call stack.

## Canonical example

Compact excerpt from the Port case (`R1-primitive-obsession.md` has the full
three-stage study — extraction, placement, testing):

```go
// Port cannot exist out of range — the constructor is the only entry.
type Port struct {
    name   string
    number int32
}

func ParsePort(name string, number int32) (Port, error) {
    if number <= 0 || number > 65535 {
        return Port{}, fmt.Errorf("port %q: %d out of range 1-65535", name, number)
    }
    return Port{name: name, number: number}, nil
}
```

Before this type existed, `p.Port > 0 && p.Port <= 65535` was duplicated across two
loops at the use site. After, there is no `IsValid()` and no re-check anywhere: the
concept of a maybe-invalid port is deleted from downstream logic, not relocated.

The same pattern for a composed object — validate dependencies once, then trust:

```go
// ❌ every method defends
type UserService struct {
    Repo Repository // exported, might be nil
}

func (s *UserService) CreateUser(ctx context.Context, u User) error {
    if s.Repo == nil { // repeated in every method; forget one → panic
        return errors.New("repo is nil")
    }
    return s.Repo.Save(ctx, u)
}

// ✅ constructor validates once; methods trust the receiver
type UserService struct {
    repo Repository // private
}

func NewUserService(repo Repository) (*UserService, error) {
    if repo == nil {
        return nil, errors.New("repo is required")
    }
    return &UserService{repo: repo}, nil
}

func (s *UserService) CreateUser(ctx context.Context, u User) error {
    return s.repo.Save(ctx, u) // no checks — an invalid service cannot exist
}
```

## Design guidance

- **Constructors are the only entry.** `ParseX(raw) (X, error)` for values built from
  unstructured input, `NewX(deps) (X, error)` for composed objects (constructors may
  carry other names — any public function returning the type qualifies). Fields stay
  private: a struct-literal or zero-value path around the constructor is a hole in
  the type.

- **Validation ownership.** A type never relies on upstream validation. "The handler
  already checked it" is not an invariant — handlers change, new call sites appear,
  and the type outlives both. A comment reading "caller must ensure X" is the
  signature of a type that does not own itself: move that sentence into the
  constructor as code.

  ```go
  // ❌ relies on callers to validate
  type Config struct {
      Host string // every caller must remember: if host == "" ...
      Port int
  }

  // ✅ owns its own validation
  func NewConfig(host string, port int) (Config, error) {
      if host == "" { return Config{}, errors.New("host required") }
      if port <= 0 || port > 65535 { return Config{}, errors.New("invalid port") }
      return Config{host: host, port: port}, nil
  }
  ```

- **Trust composed values.** Once you hold a `Port`, it is valid — never re-check it
  downstream, and never re-validate it in a composing constructor. Each type owns
  exactly its own invariants:

  ```go
  // ❌ re-validates what Host already guarantees
  func NewAddress(host Host, port Port) (Address, error) {
      if host == "" { return Address{}, errors.New("host required") } // Host owns this
      return Address{host: host, port: port}, nil
  }

  // ✅ trusts composed self-validating types — nothing left to check, no error to return
  func NewAddress(host Host, port Port) Address {
      return Address{host: host, port: port}
  }
  ```

  instead. Error positions are exempt: `nil, err` and `val, nil` are fine because the
  real value is the other one. Never pass nil into a function; then functions do not
  check parameters for nil.

  zero nil/emptiness checks on their own fields. A method validating its receiver is
  validation in the wrong place.

  `(X, error)`, migrate every literal-construction site through it.

  across methods, run them once at construction, delete them from the methods.

  self-validating and there is nothing left to check, the constructor loses its
  `error` return entirely.

  the sentinel move in `R1-primitive-obsession.md`.

   constructor for the type.

   itself.

   Violation: nil returned for a non-error value, or a function nil-checking a
   parameter instead of the value being guaranteed by construction.

6. **Does any call site pass a nil literal as a non-error argument?**
   Detection: `grep -nE '\(nil[,)]|, nil[,)]' <changed files>` — exempt error
   positions (`return X, nil`), comparisons (`== nil`, `!= nil`), and stdlib
   idioms where nil is the documented sentinel (`http.NewRequest(..., nil)` for
   a bodyless request, marshaling a nil slice/map).

   and Q2 catches the callee that defends; this catches the caller when the
   callee does neither and simply panics later. Fix on the callee's side: make
   nil unrepresentable — a concrete non-pointer parameter, or a validating
   constructor that rejects nil (see the UserService example above).

1	# Comment Noise Case: Nine Private Helpers, Nine Comments
2	
3	Demonstrates: R9 (comment policy — the visibility default)
4	
5	A real 143-line file from a JSON-RPC-over-HTTP client (anonymized), written by an
6	LLM flow before the visibility default existed. It detects which codec decoded a
7	reply body: JSON, or the client's configured non-JSON codec (msgpack). Every one
8	of its nine unexported symbols carries a comment; the file has more comment lines
9	than code lines. Each comment, judged alone, "delivers a toolbox value". The file
10	as a whole is unreadable — a human reviewer of a sibling PR called the style
11	"utterly lacking empathy for the reader".
12	
13	This is the case law for R9's visibility default: **unexported symbols get no
14	comment; the special case is one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item.**
15	
16	## The before — representative excerpts
17	
18	A 5-line comment on a private constant, with cross-repo provenance:
19	
20	```go
21	// nonJSONLeadingByteFloor is the lowest leading byte a non-JSON wire
22	// frame can start with in the leading-byte detection heuristic:
23	// JSON-RPC 2.0 envelopes always start with '{' (0x7b), and msgpack maps
24	// (fixmap, map16, map32) always start at 0x80 or above — the same
25	// boundary the legacy client's detectCodec uses.
26	nonJSONLeadingByteFloor byte = 0x80
27	```
28	
29	Decoder rings and review-defense narration on another constant:
30	
31	```go
32	// msgpackAliasContentType is the second literal spelling D-04 requires
33	// this package to accept as msgpack, alongside jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack
34	// ("application/msgpack"). Named as a single constant — not a table —
35	// per Pitfall 3: a third wire format would earn its own narrow check,
36	// not a generalized alias registry.
37	msgpackAliasContentType = "application/x-msgpack"
38	```
39	
40	Six lines on a one-line function, with forward references to its callers:
41	
42	```go
43	// trimUTF8BOM strips a leading UTF-8 BOM from data, returning data unchanged
44	// when no BOM is present. Used both to classify a reply's byte verdict
45	// (detectReplyCodec) and, for a JSON verdict, to decode it
46	// (Client.ParseResponse): encoding/json treats a BOM as an invalid leading
47	// byte rather than whitespace, so leaving it in would still fail to decode
48	// even after correct classification.
49	func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte {
50	    return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM)
51	}
52	```
53	
54	A caller list that rots on the next caller:
55	
56	```go
57	// normalizeContentType strips any ";"-delimited parameters (e.g.
58	// "; charset=binary"), trims surrounding whitespace, and lowercases the
59	// result — the shared normalization step both isMsgpackAliasContentType and
60	// replyCodecAndMismatch's header cross-check use (see codec_event.go).
61	func normalizeContentType(headerContentType string) string {
62	```
63	
64	And the centerpiece: **22 prose lines on an unexported function** — over 4× the
65	budget of an exported crossroads — ending in a sixty-word sentence:
66	
67	```go
68	// replyCodecAndMismatch returns the byte-verdict codec (identical to
69	// detectReplyCodec) plus a bool that is true when the normalized
70	// Content-Type header disagrees with that byte verdict. The byte verdict
71	// always governs the actual decode (D-04: bytes-first); mismatch is only a
72	// signal for the caller's CodecEvent, never a second decode selector.
73	//
74	// headerSaysNonJSON is true when the header exactly names nonJSON's own
75	// content type, OR — the msgpack-alias carve-out D-04 requires — the
76	// header is either msgpack spelling AND nonJSON's content type IS msgpack
77	// (the alias never claims agreement for an unrelated non-JSON codec).
78	//
79	// An empty body never mismatches: it is not a valid non-JSON envelope
80	// regardless of what the header claims.
81	//
82	// A Client with no distinct non-JSON codec configured (nonJSON is the
83	// jsonrpc.JSONCodec{} default) never mismatches either: with nothing but
84	// JSON to disagree with, an ordinary JSON reply's own "Content-Type:
85	// application/json" header would otherwise satisfy headerSaysNonJSON's
86	// literal string comparison against nonJSON.ContentType() (also
87	// "application/json"), producing a false-positive mismatch on every
88	// zero-config JSON call — a bug this guard forecloses rather than lets a
89	// caller's mismatch check ever observe.
90	func replyCodecAndMismatch(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec, headerContentType string) (jsonrpc.Codec, bool) {
91	```
92	
93	## The verdicts
94	
95	All nine symbols are unexported, so the question is existence, not size:
96	
97	| Symbol | Before | Verdict | Why |
98	|---|---|---|---|
99	| `nonJSONLeadingByteFloor` | 5 lines | one-liner survives | the WHY of the magic number ('{' is 0x7b; msgpack maps start at 0x80) — the code cannot carry it |
100	| `msgpackAliasContentType` | 5 lines | DELETE | the name and value say it; "D-04 requires" is a decoder ring; "not a table, per Pitfall 3" is review-defense narration |
101	| `utf8BOM` | 6 lines | one-liner survives | an ordering constraint: 0xEF ≥ the floor, so the BOM check must run before the leading-byte check |
102	| `trimUTF8BOM` | 6 lines | DELETE | the name is the documentation; the encoding/json quirk belongs to `replyBytesForDecode`, its only decode-side caller |
103	| `detectReplyCodec` | 7 lines | DELETE | narrated implementation ("Bounds-checked: it never indexes an empty slice") plus cross-repo provenance |
104	| `replyBytesForDecode` | 8 lines | one-liner survives | an external library quirk: encoding/json treats a BOM as an invalid leading byte, not whitespace |
105	| `normalizeContentType` | 4 lines | DELETE | the name says it; the caller list rots |
106	| `isMsgpackAliasContentType` | 5 lines | DELETE | the name says it; decoder rings and review-defense again |
107	| `replyCodecAndMismatch` | 22 lines | one-liner survives | the package's one real policy: bytes pick the decoder, the header is only a signal — the rest moves to the feature doc |
108	
109	Four one-liners survive out of nine comments; roughly 68 comment lines become 4.
110	
111	## The after
112	
113	```go
114	package jrpchttp
115	
116	import (
117	    "bytes"
118	    "strings"
119	
120	    "example.com/rpc/jsonrpc"
121	)
122	
123	const (
124	    // JSON envelopes start with '{' (0x7b); msgpack maps start at 0x80 or above.
125	    nonJSONLeadingByteFloor byte = 0x80
126	
127	    msgpackAliasContentType = "application/x-msgpack"
128	)
129	
130	// A BOM's lead byte (0xEF) is above the floor, so strip it before the leading-byte check.
131	var utf8BOM = []byte{0xEF, 0xBB, 0xBF}
132	
133	func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte {
134	    return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM)
135	}
136	
137	func detectReplyCodec(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec) jsonrpc.Codec {
138	    data = trimUTF8BOM(data)
139	    if len(data) == 0 {
140	        return jsonrpc.JSONCodec{}
141	    }
142	    if data[0] >= nonJSONLeadingByteFloor {
143	        return nonJSON
144	    }
145	
146	    return jsonrpc.JSONCodec{}
147	}
148	
149	// encoding/json treats a leading BOM as an invalid byte, not whitespace, so JSON strips it.
150	func replyBytesForDecode(codec jsonrpc.Codec, rawResponse []byte) []byte {
151	    if _, isJSON := codec.(jsonrpc.JSONCodec); isJSON {
152	        return trimUTF8BOM(rawResponse)
153	    }
154	
155	    return rawResponse
156	}
157	
158	func normalizeContentType(headerContentType string) string {
159	    contentType := headerContentType
160	    if idx := strings.IndexByte(contentType, ';'); idx >= 0 {
161	        contentType = contentType[:idx]
162	    }
163	
164	    return strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(contentType))
165	}
166	
167	func isMsgpackAliasContentType(headerContentType string) bool {
168	    switch normalizeContentType(headerContentType) {
169	    case string(jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack), msgpackAliasContentType:
170	        return true
171	    default:
172	        return false
173	    }
174	}
175	
176	// The body bytes always pick the decoder; a disagreeing Content-Type header is only reported, never trusted.
177	func replyCodecAndMismatch(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec, headerContentType string) (jsonrpc.Codec, bool) {
178	    codec := detectReplyCodec(data, nonJSON)
179	    if len(data) == 0 || nonJSON.ContentType() == jsonrpc.ContentTypeJSON {
180	        return codec, false
181	    }
182	
183	    headerSaysNonJSON := normalizeContentType(
184	        headerContentType,
185	    ) == normalizeContentType(
186	        string(nonJSON.ContentType()),
187	    ) ||
188	        (isMsgpackAliasContentType(headerContentType) && nonJSON.ContentType() == jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack)
189	    bodySaysNonJSON := codec.ContentType() != jsonrpc.ContentTypeJSON
190	
191	    return codec, headerSaysNonJSON != bodySaysNonJSON
192	}
193	```
194	
195	The knowledge that was worth keeping and did not fit a one-liner — the
196	msgpack-alias carve-out, why a JSON-only client never reports a mismatch — moves
197	to the feature doc, where the exported caller's godoc points with its See-edge.
198	The exported API (`Client.ParseResponse`, the mismatch event) is where a reader
199	meets this package; that is where the tier budgets and the See-edge live.
200	
201	## The lesson
202	
203	The tier budget caps how big a comment can be; only the visibility default
204	decides whether it should exist at all. Before this case, "Helper: 0–1 lines"
205	read as permission, and a writer in fill-the-menu mode gave every private symbol
206	its tier maximum — nine comments, each locally justified, jointly unreadable.
207	The default for unexported symbols is **zero**: the name is the documentation,
208	and a name that needs a comment wants a rename or an extraction first. The
209	special case is **one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item** — an
210	ordering constraint, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic number, the
211	package's one real policy. If a private symbol seems to need more than that one
212	line, the knowledge belongs to the exported symbol that uses it, the package
213	doc, or the feature doc.

29	## Comment Value Toolbox
30	
31	The catalog behind R9's toolbox-value test. The normative list of kinds lives in
32	R9's comment policy; **this catalog is the growable half** — when a new kind of
33	valuable comment proves itself, add it here with a worked example. Two consumers:
34	the writer picks from this toolbox when composing a comment (step 3), and the
35	`comment-critic` cites the specific toolbox item a rewrite should deliver ("swap
36	narrated implementation for the boundary contract this parsing constructor
37	needs").
38	
39	Each entry: when it earns its place, and what it looks like.
40	
41	### WHY, not WHAT
42	
43	Rationale, incident, or constraint the code cannot carry. The default value — when
44	in doubt, this is the one to reach for.
45	
46	```go
47	// ❌ ParseAddress parses an address string.            (restates the name)
48	// ✅ ParseAddress rejects ports below 1024: the collector runs unprivileged.
49	```
50	
51	### Wider context
52	
53	Where this sits architecturally; what depends on it. Earns its place on crossroads
54	symbols — the reader landing here from a grep needs to know what they're standing
55	on.
56	
57	```go
58	// ❌ Queue is a queue used by the system.               (generic filler)
59	// ✅ Every exporter ships through this queue — backpressure starts here.
60	```
61	
62	### Important use cases / flows
63	
64	When to reach for this symbol instead of its neighbors. Earns its place when the
65	choice is not obvious from the names alone.
66	
67	```go
68	// ✅ Use Snapshot for reads during a rebalance; direct reads block until it ends.
69	```
70	
71	### Boundary contract
72	
73	Dos/don'ts, valid inputs, error behavior. Earns its place on parsing constructors
74	and any API whose caller needs the contract before the first call.
75	
76	```go
77	// ✅ Accepts "3x100ms"-style specs. Zero attempts and negative delays are rejected.
78	```
79	
80	### Guarantees
81	
82	Thread safety, nil handling, invariants — promises the signature cannot express.
83	
84	```go
85	// ✅ Safe for concurrent use; callbacks run outside the lock.
86	```
87	
88	### Network edge
89	
90	The `See docs/<feature>.md` line wiring a critical point into the repo brain.
91	Near-constant: keep it whenever a feature doc exists (R9 edge policy). Free under
92	the budget.
93	
94	```go
95	// ✅ See docs/retry-policy.md for the incident and the cap math.
96	```
97	
98	### What never earns a line: provenance and decoder-ring references
99	
100	The anti-toolbox. PR numbers, review items, "the previous behavior" narration,
101	"matching what <old system> did" — change history, not behavior. The 5-year
102	reader test (R9's floor): a reader five years out cares how the product behaves
103	NOW, never which PR or review round produced it. Rewrite history as
104	present-tense rationale; keep an incident/ticket reference only when it IS the
105	rationale for a constraint.
106	
107	```go
108	// ❌ ...must be rejected, matching the legacy backend ("more than one TLS
109	//    option passed"), REST v2 (which forwarded the conflict), and the CLI's
110	//    own client-side mutual exclusion. Silently resolving by precedence —
111	//    the previous behavior — picks a TLS mode the caller didn't ask for
112	//    (PR #481 review item 5a).
113	
114	// ✅ Passing more than one TLS option is rejected (422): silently picking
115	//    one of them could apply a TLS mode the caller did not ask for.
116	```
117	
118	**Decoder-ring references** are the same failure in a different costume:
119	plan/decision/test-plan IDs ("T-04-02", "D-07"), requirement tags
120	("REQ-SVC-01"), spec section refs ("spec §4"). They fail even when the token
121	resolves inside a repo doc — a reader without the decoder ring gets nothing.
122	The fact goes in the comment as plain prose; the doc gets ONE trailing
123	See-edge; the ID stays in the doc.
124	
125	```go
126	// ❌ userResponse is the flat REST response shape for a user account
127	//    (spec §4). It deliberately has NO field for the password hash — the
128	//    response omission is structural (T-04-02), not a zero-value
129	//    coincidence ... additive to the {uid} addressing scheme (D-06/D-07).
130	
131	// ✅ userResponse is the flat REST response shape for a user account.
132	//    It has no field for the password hash or the API token, so a response
133	//    can never leak them.
134	//    See docs/accounts-api.md.
135	```
136	
137	### What never earns a line: restated repo idiom
138	
139	A comment justifying a convention the repo already applies everywhere: a
140	pointer field meaning "omitted vs explicit zero", the standard error-wrapping
141	style, the usual table-driven test shape. Each use site inherits the
142	convention silently; the explanation lives once at rung 2 (coding standards).
143	If every site carried it, the real content would drown — and the one genuine
144	WHY nearby would read as more boilerplate.
145	
146	```go
147	// ❌ // Enabled is a pointer so an omitted field is distinguishable from an
148	//    // explicit false.
149	//    Enabled *bool `json:"enabled,omitempty"`
150	
151	// ✅ Enabled *bool `json:"enabled,omitempty"`
152	```
153	
154	Test before crediting a WHY: grep the repo for the same pattern. If it appears
155	across packages with no comment, this comment restates an idiom — cut it.
156	
157	### What never earns a line: review-defense narration
158	
159	The writer arguing with an imagined reviewer: defending a design choice nobody
160	at the code line asked about, or promising the code is safe instead of letting
161	the code show it. These lines are written for the PR review round; five years
162	later they read as noise. A design choice that genuinely needs defending is
163	defended in the feature doc.
164	
165	```go
166	// ❌ Named as a single constant — not a table: a third wire format would
167	//    earn its own narrow check, not a generalized alias registry.
168	// ❌ Bounds-checked: it never indexes an empty slice.
169	
170	// ✅ (nothing — the code shows the bounds check; the design defense moves
171	//    to the feature doc if it is worth keeping at all)
172	```
173	
174	### The visibility default: private symbols get no comment
175	
176	Not an anti-entry — the existence rule the whole toolbox sits under (normative
177	in R9). The toolbox and tier menus price comments on **exported** API. An
178	unexported symbol defaults to **zero** comment lines; its name is the
179	documentation. The special case is one line carrying a very high-value toolbox
180	item: an ordering constraint, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic
181	number, the package's one real policy. Case file with nine worked verdicts:
182	`../../examples/private-comment-noise.md`.
183	
184	```go
185	// ❌ trimUTF8BOM strips a leading UTF-8 BOM from data, returning data
186	//    unchanged when no BOM is present. Used both to classify a reply's
187	//    byte verdict (detectReplyCodec) and, for a JSON verdict, to decode
188	//    it (Client.ParseResponse)...
189	func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte { return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM) }
190	
191	// ✅ (nothing — the name says it)
192	
193	// ✅ special case, one high-value line:
194	// A BOM's lead byte (0xEF) is above the floor, so strip it before the leading-byte check.
195	var utf8BOM = []byte{0xEF, 0xBB, 0xBF}
196	```
197

199	
200	## Godoc Menus
201	
202	**These are MENUS, not forms** (normative: R9's tiered comment-budget policy —
203	**1–5 prose lines** scaled to the symbol's role; blank `//` lines, the See-edge, and
204	short inline examples of 2–4 lines are free). The menus price **exported** API
205	only — unexported symbols default to no comment at all (R9's visibility
206	default; special case: one very-high-value line). The WHY is the default
207	content; the tier caps how much of a menu any one symbol can order:
208	
209	- **Helper** (small method, plain constructor, obvious accessor) → 0–1 line, or
210	  nothing; a tiny example only if it clarifies.
211	- **Contract** (parsing constructor like `ParsePort`, self-validating type, ordinary
212	  exported API) → 2–3 lines; a dos/don'ts example is free and often earns its place.
213	- **Crossroads** (entry point, orchestrator, state machine, feature front door) →
214	  up to 5 lines: WHY, architectural context, use cases.
215	
216	Overflow never stays inline — it moves to the feature doc; the
217	`See docs/<feature>.md` edge (kept whenever the doc exists) carries the pointer. A
218	crossroads that deserves more than 5 lines inline gets an expand recommendation in
219	the FEATURE report instead of extra lines — a human decides (R9's escape hatch).
220	
221	What fills the chosen menu lines comes from the [Comment Value Toolbox](#comment-value-toolbox)
222	above — every prose line must deliver one of its values, in plain English (R9's
223	three-test standard).
224	
225	### Package Godoc Menu
226	
227	Pick only the lines this package needs:
228	
229	```go
230	// Package [name] provides [high-level purpose].          <- always (one line)
231	//
232	// [1-2 sentences: what problem this solves]              <- usually
233	//
234	// Main data flow:                                        <- only if non-obvious
235	//   Input -> Validation -> Processing -> Output
236	//
237	// Core types:                                            <- multi-type packages only
238	//   - Type1: [key responsibility]
239	//
240	// Design decisions:                                      <- only where rationale exists
241	//   - [Key decision and why]
242	//
243	// See docs/[feature].md for architecture and usage.      <- whenever the doc exists
244	package name
245	```
246	
247	**The `doc.go` hatch (R9):** when a package genuinely earns more than the standard
248	budget — flow sketch, core-types list, and design decisions all pulling their
249	weight — move the package godoc to a dedicated `doc.go`, bounded at ~20–30 lines.
250	A package comment inline in a regular file stays within the standard tier budget.
251	
252	### Type Godoc Menu
253	
254	Pick per symbol kind (hints above):
255	
256	```go

258	//
259	// [WHY it exists: rationale, incident, constraint —      <- the default content
260	//  context the code cannot carry]
261	//
262	// Constraints:                                           <- self-validating types
263	//   - [validation rules, thread-safety guarantees]
264	//
265	// Use cases / flow:                                      <- logic-heavy types only
266	//   [when to reach for it, or a short flow sketch]
267	//
268	// Example:                                               <- parsing constructors:
269	//   p, err := ParsePolicy("3x100ms")  // valid              dos/don'ts inputs
270	//   _, err = ParsePolicy("0x")        // rejected: zero attempts
271	//
272	// See docs/[feature].md for the full picture.            <- whenever the doc exists
273	type TypeName struct {
274	    // ...
275	}
276	```

281	nothing:

285	//

318	## Frontmatter Templates (OKF Bundle)
319	
320	Content docs start with YAML frontmatter (R9's bundle policy — the one non-menu
321	part of any template: the required keys are not optional). A doc's index line IS
322	its `description`, so write the description as the index line you want.
323	
324	**Content doc** (feature / architecture / guide):
325	
326	```yaml
327	---
328	type: feature
329	description: why retries use capped full jitter; `Policy` API
330	# optional:
331	# title: Retry policy               # the H1 is the title; this key never replaces it
332	# generated: 2026-08-20T00:00:00Z   # OKF provenance: last substantive update
333	# tags: [resilience, retry]
334	# status: stable                    # draft | stable | deprecated
335	# stale_after: 2027-01-01           # past this date the index line gets the ⚠️ flag
336	---
337	```
338	
339	**Indexes carry no frontmatter** (OKF keeps reserved `index.md` bare). The one
340	exception is the root index (`<docroot>/index.md`), which carries the bundle
341	version — and nothing else:
342	
343	```yaml
344	---
345	okf_version: "0.2"
346	---
347	```

570	## Bootstrap Classification
571	
572	Classify each inventoried doc; the class decides its index line, grouping, and
573	frontmatter `type` (stale is a lifecycle, not a type — it keeps the class it would
574	otherwise have, expressed via `status`/`stale_after` plus the flagged line):
575	
576	| Class | Signals | Index treatment | Frontmatter `type` |
577	|-------|---------|-----------------|--------------------|
578	| **feature** | describes one capability's behavior; cites its symbols | group under its topic | `feature` |
579	| **architecture** | cross-feature structure, system-wide patterns | its own "Architecture" group | `architecture` |
580	| **guide** | setup, how-to, onboarding, runbooks | "Guides" group | `guide` |
581	| **stale** | cites symbols/packages that no longer resolve; describes removed behavior | index with a FLAGGED line (below); the flag is the advisory finding | its underlying class |
582	
583	**Stale never means unindexed** — R9's Q1 reachability invariant always wins. A stale
584	doc gets a flagged index line naming the unresolved symbol:
585	
586	```markdown
587	- [auth.md](auth.md) — ⚠️ stale: cites unresolved `TokenVerifier`
588	```
589	
590	The flag names the unresolved symbol; it cannot tell an aspirational doc (written
591	ahead of the code) from a doc for deleted code — choosing refresh (FEATURE mode) /
592	remove / keep-as-roadmap is the user's call, made from the advisory report.
593	Bootstrap never decides.
594	
595	When unsure between feature and architecture: one capability → feature; the seams
596	between capabilities → architecture.

598	### Frontmatter Migration (Brownfield)
599	
600	An existing network without frontmatter — wired by hand, or by a plugin version
601	before the OKF layer — is just another brownfield state. **Verify-or-add, never
602	duplicate**: a doc that already has conformant frontmatter is left alone; a doc
603	without gets the required keys, with `description` written as its index line
604	(add optional `generated` from the doc's last substantive git touch when
605	evident). An index
606	carrying frontmatter (written by hand, or by an older plugin version) gets it
607	stripped — the root keeps only `okf_version`. A `type` the
608	classification table cannot settle goes to the advisory report
609	(`type?: <doc> — class not inferable`) — never guessed silently. Same for
610	`conventions.md` and the check script: create or verify, and report a diverged
611	script rather than overwriting it.
612	
613	### Rung-2 Gap Criterion (BOOTSTRAP)
614	
615	FEATURE mode anchors R9 Q5 on the diff; bootstrap has no diff. Report a rung-2 gap
616	on exactly two greppable signals — nothing fuzzier:
617	
618	- **(a) Dangling intent**: a live code→docs edge points at a missing doc — the edge
619	  is evidence a doc was intended (surfaces from the Q2 code→docs grep).
620	- **(b) Undocumented front door**: a package with entry points has no doc citing any
621	  of its exported symbols.
622	
623	### Upward-Edge Anchor Heuristic (BOOTSTRAP step 5)
624	
625	Each indexed doc gets at most ONE upward edge (low density — R9 edge policy). The
626	anchor is the doc's front door, chosen in this order:
627	
628	1. **The doc's central exported symbol** — the type or constructor the doc most
629	   centrally describes: usually the first symbol its index line cites, or the type
630	   in the doc's title (`spanlogger-api.md` → the `SpanLogger` type).
631	2. **The package godoc** — when the doc spans a whole package rather than one
632	   symbol (`versioning.md` → `package version`'s doc comment).
633	3. **No confident anchor** → do not guess. Report the doc as `unwired` in the
634	   advisory findings; a wrong edge is worse than a missing one (it survives Q2 —
635	   it resolves — while pointing readers somewhere unhelpful).
636	
637	Mechanics: append the edge as the final line of the anchor's EXISTING doc comment —
638	`// See <docroot>/<file>.md for <three-to-six-word reason>.` Never restructure the
639	comment around it; never create a doc comment solely to host an edge (a naked symbol
640	is a Q5 finding for FEATURE mode, not a wiring target); confirm the package still
641	vets after the edit.

717	## Guidelines
718	
719	### Bug Fix Documentation
720	
721	Bug fixes should NEVER add changelog-style entries. Instead, update existing docs to
722	reflect correct behavior.
723	
724	**Approach:**
725	1. Find the existing documentation for the affected behavior
726	2. Update it to describe the CORRECT behavior
727	3. If no docs exist, write behavior docs as if the bug never happened
728	
729	**Example — Email Validation Bug:**
730	```
731	❌ DON'T ADD:
732	## Bug Fixes
733	- Fixed: Email validation now correctly rejects addresses without TLD
734	
735	✅ DO UPDATE existing "Validation" section:
736	## Validation
737	Email addresses must include a valid TLD (e.g., .com, .org).
738	Invalid formats return ErrInvalidEmail with descriptive message.
739	```
740	
741	**Example — Parser Edge Case:**
742	```
743	❌ DON'T ADD:
744	## v1.2.3 Changes
745	- Fixed edge case where empty input caused panic
746	
747	✅ DO UPDATE existing "Input Handling" section:
748	## Input Handling
749	Empty input returns ErrEmptyInput. All inputs are validated before parsing.
750	```
751	
752	**Why this matters:** someone reading docs in 5 years wants to know "How does
753	validation work?" — they don't care that it was broken once.
754	
755	### Managing Documentation Size
756	
757	Two distinct size rules — don't conflate them:
758	- **A single doc past ~500 lines** → split it into a folder (below).
759	- **`index.md` past ~300 lines** → map of maps (R9's index policy; form above).
760	
761	**Split signals:** doc exceeds ~500 lines; multiple distinct topics competing for
762	attention; hard to find specific information.
763	
764	**Folder structure for a large feature:**
765	```
766	docs/
767	├── index.md               # root map — links feature-name/index.md
768	└── feature-name/
769	    ├── index.md           # sub-index: one line per sub-doc
770	    ├── architecture.md    # detailed architecture, diagrams
771	    └── usage.md           # examples and patterns
772	```

774	The sub-index follows the same one-line-per-doc form; the root index links it, so
775	every sub-doc stays two hops from CLAUDE.md (R9's reachability invariant).

777	**When NOT to split:** the feature is cohesive and flows logically; splitting would
778	create orphaned fragments; sub-docs would be too thin to stand alone.

805	```go
806	// Scheduler coordinates periodic report generation across tenants.
807	// It was introduced after the v2 incident where per-tenant cron jobs
808	// drifted and overlapped, causing duplicate report emails.
809	// The scheduler holds a min-heap of next-run times and wakes on the
810	// earliest deadline. Each tick it drains all due tenants, submits
811	// them to the worker pool, and re-heaps with jittered next-run times.
812	// Jitter is +/-10% to avoid thundering herd on shared storage.
813	// Thread safety: all public methods lock the internal mutex; callbacks
814	// run outside the lock. Do not call Schedule from inside a callback.
815	// See docs/report-scheduling.md.
816	type Scheduler struct { /* ... */ }
817	```

819	narration (rung-2 material at best) drowning the two facts a reader at this symbol
820	actually needs. Reviewers scroll past comments like this, then miss the one that
821	matters.

828	// next-run times replaced them.

830	// See docs/report-scheduling.md for the tick flow and jitter math.
831	type Scheduler struct { /* ... */ }

917	### Common Documentation Scenarios
